questions.text: What does matching a tool descriptor to its previously approved hash establish?

options.A: The descriptor cannot contain malicious instructions.
options.B: The server’s display name is an authenticated publisher identity.
options.C: The descriptor has stayed unchanged, while its safety still depends on review.
options.D: The executor automatically enforces the permissions described in its annotations.

questions.explanation: Hash equality proves stability of the pinned bytes, not that the original descriptor was safe or that its claims are enforced.

questions.text: An approved tool keeps its name and description but changes inputSchema. Which admission control detects this change?

options.A: Pin and compare a canonical digest of the complete descriptor.
options.B: Scan only the description for known injection phrases.
options.C: Trust the tool because its qualified name is unchanged.
options.D: Use clientInfo.version as permission to accept schema changes.

questions.explanation: Whole-descriptor pinning includes the schema. A description-only scan or hash misses changes to other fields.

questions.text: In SecurityGateway.handle, _visible_tools scans descriptors for tools/list, but the tools/call branch routes directly by params.name. After notes.search is changed and hidden from the list, what does a direct valid tools/call to notes.search do?

options.A: It fails the approved-digest check before reaching the handler.
options.B: It returns the hard-coded search result because dispatch does not rescan the descriptor.
options.C: It automatically updates the approved hash before executing search.
options.D: It returns method-not-found because hidden tools are removed from the method table.

questions.explanation: The sample checks visibility during listing, but the direct call branch still matches notes.search and returns its fixed result. Discovery filtering alone does not enforce admission at dispatch.
